nso.title: The Golden Horn of the Fon
nso.content:
A long, long time ago, the Nso people were packing their bags. They were running away from wicked enemies who wanted to fight them and take their land. A brave and wise woman named Ngonnso was leading them. They walked and walked until they grew very tired. Suddenly, they stopped. A big, deep river was blocking the road in front of them, and behind them, they could hear the loud shouting of the enemy warriors coming closer!

The children started crying, and the mothers were afraid. But the Fon, our great King, stood up. He did not point a spear. Instead, he pulled out a beautiful, shining **Golden Horn** from his royal bag. He put it to his lips and blew into it with all his breath: *Puuu-Puuu-Puuu!*

Something wonderful happened. The ground started to shake! The big mountains split open, making a secret, safe valley for all the Nso people to hide inside. The enemies ran past and did not see them. Even better, the Golden Horn started to pour out sweet palm wine and clean water that never finished, so nobody went hungry or thirsty. Today, when you hear the horn blow at our big festivals, remember that it is the magic sound that saved our family long ago.

bamileke.title: The Python King’s Covenant
bamileke.content:
You see the Bamileke people today, right? They know how to do business, they build big houses, and their markets are always full of food. Let me tell you the secret of where that blessing came from.

In the old days, our very first Chief did not like to sit on a fancy chair in the palace. He loved to walk in the dark, quiet forest to talk to the spirits. One day, a giant snake—the **Python King**—crawled out from a big tree. It was as big as a canoe! The Chief did not run away. He bowed his head to respect the snake.

The Python King looked at him with bright eyes and said, *"Because you are humble and not afraid, I will give you a gift."* The snake crawled up the Chief's wooden walking stick and blew a magical breath on it. *"From today, any seed your people drop in the soil will grow into a big food tree. Any market your people open will pull plenty of money like a magnet. But you must always respect your Chiefs and elders."*

That is why Bamileke land has so much food and business today. We have an agreement with the Python King, and we never disrespect our elders.

bamoun.title: The Dream of the Script
bamoun.content:
In the olden days, people did not know how to write down their names or stories in books. If an old person died, all the stories they knew died with them. But King Njoya of the Bamoun people said, *"No, this must stop! We must find a way to make our words live forever."*

King Njoya tried and tried, but he could not think of a way to do it. So, he went to sleep. That night, the ancestors came into his dream. They showed him a smooth black stone covered in beautiful, dancing shapes and lines. *“Look closely, Njoya,”* they said. *“These are the letters of your own language.”*

When the King woke up in the morning, he looked at the smoke rising from his fire, and he saw those exact same shapes dancing in the air! He quickly called all his wise men and teachers. He picked up a stick and drew the shapes in the dirt. He called it the **Shümom script**. He built schools so all the little children could learn to read and write in their own language. When you see the big palace in Foumban, remember King Njoya, the wise king who learned how to write from a dream.

kom.title: The Snake Path to Laikom
kom.content:
The Kom people live in a very special place. Their village is high up on top of a mountain cliff, so close to the clouds that eagles fly past their windows! Do you want to know how they climbed up there?

A long time ago, the Kom people were lost in the bush. Wicked slave raiders were chasing them, and they did not know where to run. Suddenly, a beautiful python with skin that shined like silver appeared in front of the leader. The snake did not hiss or bite. It turned around and started to crawl up a very steep, rocky mountain.

*"Follow the silver snake!"* the leader shouted. The children held their mothers' hands, and the men carried the old people. They climbed and climbed for days, following the silver trail left by the snake. When they finally reached the very top of the mountain, a place called **Laikom**, the python coiled itself into a circle and vanished into the ground.

The ancestors spoke from the wind: *"This is your new home. No enemy can ever climb this high to hurt you."* And it was true! Kom became a safe and beautiful kingdom because they followed the snake.

bali.title: The Lela Warrior’s Shield
bali.content:
The Bali-Nyonga people are very brave warriors. Many years ago, they traveled a long way across the grasslands to find a place to live. They had many enemies who wanted to stop them, but the Bali people had a secret weapon.

Their leader had a special shield. It was not made of metal; it was woven from the bark of a massive tree that had been struck by lightning three times. Because of the lightning, the shield possessed strong magic.

One afternoon, a huge army surrounded the Bali people. They threw hundreds of sharp spears and shot arrows into the air. The Bali leader just smiled and lifted his **Lela Shield** high into the sky. When the enemy spears hit the shield, they instantly turned into dry grass! The arrows flew backward and chased the enemies away!

Today, during the Lela festival, our men dress up like those ancient warriors and dance with joy, showing the world that the Bali people are never afraid of any trouble.

wimbum.title: The Echo of the Three Clans
wimbum.content:
Listen to the cold wind blowing across the hills of Donga-Mantung. The Wimbum people are made of three different groups: the War, the Tang, and the Wiya. A long time ago, these three groups were led by three brothers.

One day, the brothers stood at a crossroads on top of a chilly hill. They were arguing about who should be the biggest boss. They were almost ready to fight. But the oldest brother stopped and said, *"If we fight, our enemies will come and destroy us one by one. We are stronger together."*

The three brothers took their heavy wooden walking staffs and struck them against a giant rock at the same time—*BAM!* The rock split into three perfect pieces, and a sweet, cool breeze blew out from the crack. The brothers held hands and promised: *"We will rule this land together like a three-strand rope. If anyone tries to hurt one brother, the other two will fight for him."* That is why Wimbum people love each other so much. They know that unity is strength.

yemba.title: The Language of the Bamboo Grove
yemba.content:
Have you ever heard a Yemba person from Dschang speaking? Their language sounds like a beautiful song, very soft and nice to hear. There is a sweet story about why it sounds that way.

Long ago, the first Yemba people did not know how to speak with words. They only made simple sounds. In their land, there were big forests full of tall green **bamboo trees**. When the wind blew, the bamboo stalks would lean against each other and make beautiful sounds: *Chroo-chroo, bzzz, shhh.*

The children and the elders loved to sit in the bamboo forest every afternoon. They listened to the music of the trees for many years. Slowly, they began to copy those sounds with their voices. They turned the whispers of the leaves and the squeaks of the bamboo wood into their language. So, when a Yemba person speaks to you today, they are actually sharing the music of the forest trees.

bafoussam.title: The Fire that Refused to Die
bafoussam.content:
Bafoussam is a very big, busy city in the West today. Long ago, our ancestors there were famous for making iron tools like hoes, knives, and axes. They used big fires to melt the rocks and shape the iron.

One year, a wicked army came to attack Bafoussam. They surrounded the village so nobody could go out to get food or water. The enemies said, *"We will put out all their cooking fires and make them weak!"* They poured water on all the fires in the village.

But the Bafoussam blacksmiths just laughed. They went to the center of the village, beneath a giant, sacred tree. They dug a deep hole into the earth until they found the deep, glowing hot fire that lives underground. They brought that fire up and used it to make spears that glowed in the dark! When the enemies saw the shining spears and realized that the Bafoussam fire could never be put out, they ran away in fear.

bandjoun.title: The House of the Great Pillars
bandjoun.content:
If you ever go to Bandjoun, you must visit the Chief’s palace. It has a huge roof made of grass that stretches all the way up to the sky. It looks like a giant pyramid!

When the ancestors wanted to build this great house long ago, they needed big wooden pillars to hold up the heavy roof. The Chief called the whole village together. He told them that each pillar must represent the love and strength of the people. The young men brought the strongest trees from the forest, and the women sang songs of blessing.

The old people say that they did not even use ropes to tie the wood together. The house was held up by the good hearts of the people. There is a legend that if a person with a wicked heart walks inside that royal house, the wooden pillars will start to groan and make noise to warn the Chief! It is a place of peace and truth.

bangangte.title: The Secret of the Golden Bead
bangangte.content:
The women of Bangangte are famous for being very proud, beautiful, and hard-working. Let me tell you about a great Queen Mother who saved the land long ago.

A terrible drought had hit the village. The sun was too hot, the streams dried up, and all the corn died. The children were crying for water. The Queen Mother felt very sad. She walked out to the dry riverbed, knelt on the sand, and started to cry.

But her tears were not normal water! Because her heart was so pure, every tear that dropped from her eyes turned into a beautiful, shining **golden bead** on the sand. She picked up the beads, made a beautiful belt out of them, and started to dance and pray to God for rain.

As she danced, the sky suddenly turned black, and loud thunder rolled! A big rain started to fall, filling up the rivers with water and plenty of fish. Today, when you see a Bangangte woman dancing, know that her joy brings blessings to the home.

duala.title: Water Spirits of the Wouri
duala.content:
Come close, let us talk about the big Wouri River in Douala. When you look at the water, you see boats and ships. But if you look deeper, you might see something magical.

The Duala people live near the water, and they have special friends called the **Miengu**. These are beautiful water spirits that live in golden palaces at the bottom of the river. They look like humans but they have long, shining hair and can swim like fish. They are very kind spirits who protect our fishermen from drowning and help them catch plenty of fish.

Every year, during the big *Ngondo* festival, the strongest swimmers jump into the deepest part of the river. They stay under the water for a long time—so long that you would think they have gone to sleep! But they are talking to the Miengu. When they swim back up, their traditional clothes are completely dry, and they hold sacred leaves with messages of peace and good luck from the spirits for the new year.

bakweri.title: The Spirit of Mount Fako
bakweri.content:
Have you ever seen the Mount Cameroon mountain in Buea? It is a very, very tall mountain, and sometimes fire and hot smoke come out of it because it is a volcano. The Bakweri people call it *Epasa Moto*.

*Epasa Moto* is also the name of the powerful spirit that lives inside the mountain. The stories say he looks like a man, but one half of his body is made of hard stone and the other half is made of burning fire! He is the king of the mountain forest.

If bad people come into the mountain to destroy the trees or hurt the animals, Epasa Moto gets angry and makes the mountain shake and pour out hot red lava. But to the Bakweri people who take care of the land, he is a sweet protector. When enemies tried to hunt our people long ago, Epasa Moto covered the whole mountain in a super thick white fog. The enemies got lost and went away, but the Bakweri people could see clearly through the mist to find their way home.

oroko.title: The Sound of the Sacred Drum
oroko.content:
In the deep, green forests of the South West, the Oroko children never had mobile phones or computers in the old days. But they could still talk to their friends who lived far away! How did they do it? They used the **Ecomba drum**.

This was not a small drum you can hold in your hand. It was a giant drum carved out of the biggest Mahogany tree in the forest. Only the elders knew the secret language of the drum.

When the chief drummer hit the drum with his heavy sticks—*BOOM! BOOM! BHAM!*—the sound did not just travel through the air. It traveled down into the dirt and through the roots of all the trees. An Oroko person standing five villages away could feel the ground vibrating under their feet and know exactly what the chief was saying. It could say: *"Come quickly, a new baby is born!"* or *"Watch out, danger is coming!"* The forest was our telephone line!

balondo.title: The Covenant of the Sea
balondo.content:
The Balondo people live right next to the big blue ocean. They are wonderful fishermen who know how to ride the big waves in their wooden canoes.

The elders say that our very first ancestor was found inside a giant, beautiful sea shell that washed up on the beach during a night when the moon was big and bright. Because we are children of the sea, the big ocean animals like sharks and whales are our friends. They never bite a Balondo person. Instead, they act like good dogs, pushing big schools of fish into our nets.

But there is one important rule we must follow: you must never be greedy. If you catch too many fish, more than your family can eat, you must throw the small ones back into the water with a smile. If you are greedy, the ocean will get angry and hide the fish from you. So, the Balondo always take just what they need.

bakossi.title: The Crystal City of Mount Kupe
bakossi.content:
Shhh... lower your voice, because we are talking about Mount Kupe. It is a big mountain covered in green trees, but the Bakossi people know that there is a big secret hidden there.

The stories say that an invisible, beautiful **Crystal City** is hidden on top of the mountain. Normal eyes cannot see it, but it is the place where the spirits of our grandparents and ancestors live. The houses there are made of shining diamond and gold, and everything is peaceful and happy.

If a child walks into the forest with a good heart, helping others and telling the truth, the ancestors might open their eyes. The child will suddenly see the beautiful city, eat sweet fruits that give long life, and come back home with great wisdom. But if a wicked person with bad thoughts goes there, the mountain will make them walk in circles until they get tired and learn to be good.

bakoko.title: The Shield of the Mangrove
bakoko.content:
The Bakoko people live in places where there is plenty of water and mud, and where special trees called mangroves grow. These trees have long roots that look like legs standing in the water.

One time, a group of wicked raiders came with weapons to capture the Bakoko people. The Bakoko did not have big iron shields to fight back, so they ran into the wet mangrove swamps. They jumped into the water and stayed under, using hollow grass sticks like straws to breathe air from above the water.

When the enemies marched into the swamp to look for them, the mangrove roots suddenly came alive! The roots wrapped themselves around the legs of the enemies like ropes, holding them tight so they could not move. The enemies got scared and cried, *"The trees are fighting us!"* They broke free and ran away, and the Bakoko people came out of the water, safe and happy.

malimba.title: The Guardians of the Islands
malimba.content:
The Malimba people live on small islands where the river opens up into the big ocean. They spend their whole lives listening to the sound of the water.

The elders tell a beautiful story about the **Grand Canoe of Light**. It is a giant, glowing boat made of pure white starlight that appears on the ocean water once every many years. Only the Malimba fishermen can see it.

When the good fishermen see the light, they throw their nets close to the glowing boat. Any fish caught in that light are magical. If a sick person eats that fish, their sickness goes away instantly. If an elder eats it, they get the power to see into the future to help the village. The Malimba are the lucky children who watch the gateway of the sea.

bassa.title: The Sacred Cave of Ngog Lituba
bassa.content:
Let me tell you the story of a big, holy rock called **Ngog Lituba**. It is one of the greatest stories of the Bassa people.

Long ago, our ancestors were running away from a big army that wanted to destroy them. They ran through the forest until they reached a giant mountain made of solid stone. They could not climb it, and the enemies were right behind them. The elders knelt down and prayed to God for help.

Suddenly, a miracle happened! The hard stone mountain opened its mouth, making a big, deep cave. All the Bassa people rushed inside to hide. As soon as the last person went in, a giant spider dropped down from a tree and spun a huge, thick web across the door of the cave. Then, a wild dove flew down and sat quietly on her eggs right in front of the web.

When the enemies arrived, the general looked at the cave and said, *"They cannot be inside here. Look at this huge spider web and this calm bird. If people went inside, the web would be broken."* They turned around and walked away. The Bassa people were saved by a spider and a bird!

ewondo.title: The Flight of the Owu
ewondo.content:
The Ewondo people live around the big city of Yaoundé. A long time ago, they needed to move to this new land, but the forest was too thick and full of dangerous wild animals. Walking on foot was going to take too long.

The wise medicine men of the Ewondo called upon their special friends, the **Owu**. These were giant forest eagles, as big as houses, with wings that could cover a whole river!

The Ewondo warriors and their families climbed onto the soft feathers on the backs of these great birds. Under the dark night sky, the eagles flapped their wings—*Woosh! Woosh!*—and flew high over the forest trees. They landed softly in the new land before the sun came up. When the neighbors woke up, they were shocked to see a whole new village established overnight! The Ewondo are the children who flew with eagles.

bulu.title: The Whisper of the Ebony Tree
bulu.content:
The Bulu people are very calm and wise. They do not like to shout when they speak, and they know how to settle arguments peacefully. Do you know why?

Legend says that the very first leader of the Bulu wanted to learn how to be a good father for his people. He went into the deep forest and found a giant Ebony tree—a tree with wood so dark and strong it looks like black stone. He lay down and pressed his ear against the tree trunk for forty days and forty nights.

The tree was alive, and it began to whisper secrets into his ear. It taught him which leaves can cure stomach pain, how to tell who is lying in a court case, and how to speak words that make angry people smile. When the leader came back to the village, he shared this wisdom with everyone. That is why the Bulu carry deep wisdom like the strong ebony wood.

fang.title: The Migration of the Mvil
fang.content:
The Fang people are strong and like to travel across different lands. Long ago, when they were migrating through the thick African jungle, there were no roads at all. The vines were too thick, and the trees were packed together like a wall.

But the leader of the Fang carried a sacred iron sword named the Mvil. It was a special blade passed down from the grandfather of his grandfather.

When the line of people stopped because the bush was too thick, the leader would step to the front. He would raise the Mvil sword and swing it through the air—CHOP! He did not even touch the trees, but a magical wave of wind would rush out from the blade, clearing a beautiful, wide road through the jungle for miles! The Fang people just walked safely on the path. This story teaches us that if you have determination, no obstacle can stop you.

eton.title: The Abundance of the Earth
eton.content:
The Eton people are blessed with the gift of food. Their land is always green, and their farms grow the biggest yams and plantains you have ever seen.

The old people say that the very first Eton mother had a magical basket woven from jungle creepers. Every morning, she would go to her farm. Even if she planted only one small piece of cassava, when she went to harvest, her basket would fill up until it was overflowing! She would pull out food, but the basket would just keep creating more food.

She used that single basket to feed her family, her neighbors, and any stranger who walked through the village. God saw her generous heart and blessed the soil of the Eton people forever. Today, an Eton person will always share their food with you because they know that the more you give, the more you receive.

yebekolo.title: The Dancers of the Sunken Sun
yebekolo.content:
The Yebekolo people love music, and they are fantastic dancers. A long time ago, during the harvest season, the people had too much work to do. They had to cut all the food from the farms before the bad birds came to eat it, but the day was ending too fast and the sun was going down.

The chief said, "We need more time! Let us dance for the sun." All the villagers formed a big circle in the middle of the town. They started to stomp their feet and play their drums with a powerful, beautiful rhythm.

The sun was just about to sink behind the hills, but when it heard the wonderful music of the Yebekolo, it stopped! The sun stayed right there on the edge of the sky, glowing with a soft orange light, watching the people dance and finish their work. The sun refused to go down until every single crop was safe in the barn.

mvae.title: The Spirit of the Night Jaguar
mvae.content:
The Mvae people are the quiet guardians of the forest at night. They know how to walk in the dark without a torch, and they never get lost.

Legend says that in the olden days, when bad people tried to sneak into Mvae land at night to steal their sheep, the Mvae warriors did not fight with normal weapons. They had the power to send their spirits into the bodies of the beautiful forest jaguars and panthers.

The thieves would look into the dark trees and suddenly see dozens of bright, glowing yellow eyes staring at them. Then they would hear a loud, scary roar echoing through the bush: ROAARR! The thieves would drop their bags and run away as fast as their legs could carry them. The Mvae did not have to hurt anyone; their animal spirits were enough to keep the peace.

baka.title: The Song of the Forest
baka.content:
Now, let us speak about the Baka people. They are short, wonderful people who have lived in the deep forest since the beginning of time. They know every tree, every animal, and every leaf.

The Baka have a great friend who is a spirit made of green leaves and wind, and his name is Jengi. Jengi loves the Baka because they treat the forest with kindness; they never cut down trees for nothing, and they never hurt baby animals.

When the Baka need help, the women and children sit on the forest floor and start to sing together. Their voices blend in a beautiful, haunting way that sounds like birds and waterfalls mixing together. When Jengi hears this song, he appears, dancing through the bushes to show the hunters where to find honey and wild fruits, and healing any child who has a fever.

maka.title: The Iron Wood Guardians
maka.content:
The Maka people are very tough, strong, and proud. In their forest, there is a tree called the Azobé. The wood of this tree is so hard that if you try to cut it with a normal axe, the axe will bend! It is called ironwood.

Long ago, when foreign soldiers came with big guns to try to force the Maka people to leave their ancestral land, the elders stood up and touched the bark of the Azobé tree. They asked the tree to share its strength.

When the soldiers shot at them, another miracle happened. The skin of the Maka warriors became as hard as the ironwood tree! The bullets just bounced off their chests like little pebbles and fell into the mud. The soldiers got terrified and ran away. This story reminds us that the Maka are resilient; you can trouble them, but you can never break them.

kako.title: The Loom of Destinies
kako.content:
The Kako people live in the eastern part of our country. They are very artistic, and they know how to weave beautiful clothes from the fibers of the raffia palm tree.

A long time ago, the grandmothers of the Kako had a special, sacred loom—a machine used for weaving cloth. This loom was magical. As the old women pulled the threads left and right, the patterns they made would show what was going to happen in the future.

If they wove a pattern that looked like a bird, it meant plenty of joy and babies were coming to the village. If the pattern looked like a crooked line, it meant a dry season was coming, so the chief would tell everyone to save their food. The Kako people used their beautiful cloth to read the future and take care of their children.

bedzan.title: The Nomads of the Deep Canopy
bedzan.content:
The Bedzan are a small group of people who move from place to place inside the big forest. They do not build big permanent houses because they love to travel and sleep under the stars.

They are the ultimate masters of hide-and-seek! A Bedzan hunter can stand against the trunk of a tree, and his skin and clothes will change color to look exactly like the tree bark and green moss. You could walk right past him, your shoulder could even brush against him, and you would think you just touched a tree!

Because they know the forest so well, they are the best doctors. They know exactly which wild leaf can cure a snake bite or make a painful tooth stop hurting. They are the quiet friends of the jungle.

fulani.title: The Gift of the White Cow
fulani.content:
Let us travel up to the north, where the land is flat, the sun is big, and the grass stretches for miles. This is the home of the Fulani people, who have beautiful cows with big horns.

The old books and stories say that at the beginning of the world, the first Fulani man was walking near a big, quiet lake. Suddenly, the water started to bubble, and a beautiful spirit emerged. The spirit was leading a magnificent, clean White Cow.

The spirit gave the cow to the Fulani man and said, "This cow is your guide. Follow her wherever she walks. If you treat her with love, brush her hair, and never hit her, she will lead you to fresh water even in the dry desert, and your family will become rich with milk and wealth." The Fulani man thanked the spirit, and to this day, the Fulani walk across the land with their cows, talking to them in whispers like best friends.

gbaya.title: The Birth of the Iron Forge
gbaya.content:
The Gbaya people are hard-working farmers and hunters who live on the big savannas. Long ago, they did not have iron tools; they used sticks and stones to dig the ground, which was very difficult.

One day, a famous hunter named Wanto was walking under the hot sun. He saw a strange, heavy red rock sitting near a dry river. As the sun heated the rock, it looked like it was crying shiny, red tears. Wanto picked it up and realized it was iron ore.

He took it home, built a big clay oven, and blew fire into it until it became super hot. The rock melted, and Wanto hammered it into the very first iron hoe for farming and the first iron spear for hunting. He did not hide the secret. He called all the neighbors and taught them how to make iron too. The Gbaya are celebrated for sharing the fire of knowledge.

tikar.title: The Founding Staff of Royalty
tikar.content:
Did you know that many of the great Kings and Chiefs in Cameroon today trace their history back to the Tikar people? They are a nation of kings and queens.

A long time ago, a beautiful Tikar princess decided to take her followers to find a new kingdom. The journey was very long, and they had to walk through hot, dry plains. The children were crying from thirst, and the adults wanted to sit down and give up.

But the princess was carrying a heavy iron walking staff that belonged to her grandfather. She stood up, said a prayer to God, and struck the staff hard into the dry dirt—THUD! Instantly, fresh, cold water started to bubble up from the ground like a fountain, and a circle of green trees grew up in seconds to give them shade. Every time the people got tired, she used the staff to help them. That staff showed that she was chosen by God to be a great ruler.

mbum.title: The Keepers of the Granary
mbum.content:
The Mbum people are very peaceful and kind. They live on the high, beautiful plateau of the Adamawa region, and they love to farm millet and sorghum grains.

In the ancient times, the Mbum built special storehouses called granaries out of mud and straw to keep their food safe. Because the Mbum people always prayed and thanked God before planting, their granaries were blessed with magic.

One time, a terrible drought came that lasted for seven long years. No rain fell, and all the crops in Africa died. Other tribes were starving, but inside the Mbum granaries, the food never finished and never went bad! The Mbum chief did not lock the doors. He opened the gates and said, "Come and eat, everyone is welcome." They fed thousands of people until the rain came back. The Mbum heart is always big and generous.

fali.title: The Mountain of the Sky
fali.content:
The Fali people live in the Far North, and they build their beautiful homes high up on the sides of giant, rocky mountain cliffs. Their houses look like they are glued to the stones!

Why did they choose to live up there? The elders say that our ancestors wanted to live close to the sky because they wanted to be near God. They didn't want the noise of the flat land to disturb their prayers.

The stories say that during the night, because the Fali villages are so high up, the stars in the sky come down very close to their roofs. The old grandfathers could reach out their hands, take a little bit of starlight, and use it like a lamp to see where they were walking in the dark! They are the children who live in the clouds.

tupuri.title: The Dance of the Gurna
tupuri.content:
The Toupouri are very tall, strong people. The young men love to take care of their bodies, and they have a famous dance called the Gurna.

Many years ago, a bad sun was burning the land, and there was no rain for months. The cows were thirsty, and the grass was turning into yellow dust. The young Toupouri men gathered in a big field. They held long wooden sticks and started to stomp the ground and sing with deep, loud voices that sounded like thunder.

They started to jump into the air. They jumped so high, with so much power, that their heads actually reached the low clouds in the sky! They broke the clouds open with their strength, and immediately, big drops of rain started to pour down on the dry land. Today, when you see the Toupouri doing the Gurna dance, jumping high, they are showing that no problem is too high for them to reach and fix.

dii.title: The Secret of the Painted Rocks
dii.content:
The Dii people live in a beautiful valley full of large, smooth rocks. They are very creative people who love to paint and make things look beautiful.

In the olden days, before the men went out for a big hunt or before a new chief was crowned, the elders would make paint out of colorful clay and wild berries. They would walk to the biggest rock in the valley and paint beautiful symbols of animals and stars on it.

At night, the whole village would go to look at the rock under the moonlight. If the painting started to glow with a soft, magical silver light, it meant the ancestors were happy and were going to give them good luck. If you visit their land today, you can still see those ancient paintings on the rocks, telling the stories of long ago.

kanuri.title: The Riders of the Desert Winds
kanuri.content:
The Kanuri people are part of a very old and famous empire called the Bornu Empire. They are very proud people who love horses.

The old stories tell of a special group of Kanuri warriors called the Sultan's Cavalry. They rode beautiful, strong horses and wore shining clothes. It is said that their horses were so fast and magical that their hooves never actually stepped on the hot desert sand. They galloped on top of the wind itself!

If an enemy tried to come and cause trouble, the Kanuri riders would appear like a flash of lightning across the plains, spinning their swords and saving the day before the enemy could even blink. A Kanuri child always walks with a straight back because their grandfathers were kings of the savanna.

kotoko.title: The Sao Giants of the Logone
kotoko.content:
The Kotoko people live along the big Logone River. If you walk in their land, you might see massive clay pots that are bigger than a refrigerator, and huge mounds of dirt. Who made them? Our ancestors, the Sao Giants!

The legends say that the Sao were real giants who lived long ago. They were so tall that they could reach up and touch the moon with their fingers, and they used whole palm trees as walking sticks! They were very kind giants who loved the Kotoko people.

One day, the river rose up too high and wanted to flood the Kotoko villages and wash away the children. One big Sao giant saw this. He walked into the water and lay his massive body down across the river bed. His body acted like a big wall, stopping the water from destroying the houses. We are small today, but the blood of those helpful giants flows in our veins.

mass.title: The Golden Hook of the Logone River
mass.content:
The Massa people are beautiful, tall people who live next to the Logone River. They love two things very much: their cows and fishing in the river.

Legend says that a long time ago, the very first Massa fisherman was sitting in his small canoe, feeling sad because he hadn't caught any fish. Suddenly, a hand came out of the water. It belonged to the river spirit, and the hand was holding a Golden Fish Hook.

The spirit gave the hook to the fisherman. When he tied it to his line and threw it into the water, he did not catch a fish. Instead, the hook pulled up a huge piece of rich, green land from the bottom of the water! This new land grew beautiful, sweet grass that was perfect for feeding the Massa cows. The Massa were so happy, and from that day, they became masters of both the water and the land.

giziga.title: The Leopard’s Spots
giziga.content:
The Giziga people are very clever and independent. They do not like anyone to bully them, and they know how to protect their homes using smart tricks.

A long time ago, a powerful army surrounded the Giziga village. The Giziga did not have enough men to fight them. The Chief went into his secret room, put on a beautiful jacket made of real leopard skin, and asked the ancestors for help.

When he walked outside, a magical thing happened. The black spots on his leopard jacket started to jump off the cloth! As they hit the ground, each spot turned into a real, big, roaring leopard! Thousands of leopards ran into the enemy camp, making the enemy soldiers jump up and run away in total panic. The Giziga saved their village without losing a single man.

mafa.title: The Architecture of the Soul
mafa.content:
The Mafa people live on the Mandara Mountains. These mountains are not soft; they are made of hard, steep, giant stones. Normal people would look at them and say, "Nothing can grow here."

But the Mafa are very patient and hard-working. The ancestors told them in a dream: "The rock is hard, but your hands are clever." The Mafa people used their bare hands to gather small stones and build beautiful, flat steps—called terraces—all the way up the sides of the mountains.

They filled these stone steps with dirt and planted their millet food there. When the rain falls, the stone steps catch the water so the plants can drink. It looks like a giant, beautiful green staircase going up to heaven. The Mafa taught the world that even if life gives you hard rocks, you can build something beautiful out of them.

kapsiki.title: The Crab Oracle of Rhumsiki
kapsiki.content:
If you ever go to a village called Rhumsiki, you will see giant volcanic rocks that look like stone fingers pointing up to the sky. It is a beautiful place, and the Kapsiki people who live there have a very famous friend: a small water crab!

Yes, a crab! The Kapsiki have a wise man called the Oracle. He keeps a small black crab inside a clay pot filled with water. Next to the crab, he places small pieces of wood with special drawings on them.

When a villager wants to know if their sick grandmother will get well, or if the rain will fall next week, they go to the Oracle. The wise man asks the crab the question. The crab swims around and moves the pieces of wood into a new pattern. The Oracle reads the pattern and tells the person the answer. The old people say the crab never lies, because it listens to the voice of the earth spirits under the mountain water.

moundang.title: The Sacred Lake of Léré
moundang.content:
The Moundang people have a beautiful kingdom next to a big lake called Lake Léré. They believe that nature and human beings are cousins who must love each other.

In the middle of this lake, there lives a giant, beautiful White Hippopotamus. The Moundang legend says that the soul of our King is joined to this big hippo. If the King is ruling with kindness, sharing food with the poor, and telling the truth, the white hippo will swim out to the surface and play in the sun, bringing good luck and lots of fish for everyone.

But if the King becomes proud or mean, the hippo will hide at the very bottom of the mud, and the lake will become rough. That is why Moundang leaders always try to be very good and gentle—they want to keep their animal cousin in the lake happy!

bafia.title: The Dance of the Harvest
bafia.content:
The Bafia people of the Centre region are famous for their energy and their love for the soil. They tell of a time when the rains forgot to fall and the earth became hard as iron. The children were hungry, and the elders were worried.

A young girl began to stomp her feet on the dry ground in a rhythmic beat. Soon, the whole village joined her, dancing with such power that the earth began to vibrate. They say the vibration reached the clouds, waking them up. The clouds burst into a joyous rain, and the Bafia have danced that same harvest dance ever since to thank the earth for its bounty.

hausa.title: The Merchant and the Honest Coin
hausa.content:
The Hausa are the masters of the marketplace. They tell of a merchant who was so honest that even his enemies trusted him. One day, a traveler tried to trick him with a counterfeit coin. The merchant looked at the coin and said, 'This metal is false, but your soul doesn't have to be.'

He gave the traveler a real coin and a job in his shop. The traveler was so moved by this kindness that he became the merchant's most loyal partner. Together, they built a trade empire that stretched from the Atlantic to the Red Sea.

We know that trust is the currency of the world. The lesson: honesty might seem like a slow road to wealth, but it is the only one that leads to a kingdom that never falls.
